q: Which investigation is most helpful in assessing a child with an acute asthma attack?
o: Arterial blood gas in every child
e: Pulse oximetry is the best bedside test of severity.

q: The most significant risk factor for childhood asthma is:
e: Atopy and parental asthma are the strongest risk factors.

q: In acute severe asthma, all are true EXCEPT:

e: Little air moves, so the wheeze disappears.

q: All are chest X-ray findings in asthma EXCEPT:
e: Hyperinflation is typical; the heart is normal.

q: In an acute attack, a normal or rising PaCO₂ means:
o: The child is tiring and needs intensive care
e: Early attacks have low PaCO₂; a normal PaCO₂ is a danger sign.

q: A 16-year-old known asthmatic is short of breath. Which feature suggests severe asthma?
e: Pulsus paradoxus > 10–20 mmHg indicates severe obstruction.

q: According to GINA 2026, a 9-year-old with asthma symptoms twice a week should receive:
o: An ICS-containing treatment, not salbutamol alone
e: SABA-only treatment is no longer advised for children 6–11.
k: not be treated with salbutamol alone

q: Before stepping up treatment in a poorly controlled asthmatic child, the first thing to check is:
e: Most poor control is due to technique, adherence or triggers.

q: A 7-year-old in a severe asthma attack has not improved after salbutamol, ipratropium and IV hydrocortisone. The next drug is:
An asthmatic child on inhaled fluticasone develops white plaques in the mouth. Advice is:
o: Use a spacer and rinse the mouth after each dose
e: Oral thrush from ICS is reduced by a spacer and mouth rinsing.

q: The best device for a 2-year-old with asthma is:
o: MDI with spacer and face mask
